title: Lentil Dahl
subtitle: slow-simmered spiced lentils with a tarka finish
excerpt: Dahl is one of the most widely eaten dishes on earth. This version uses green lentils simmered with tomatoes and spices, finished with a tarka -- hot oil infused with cumin seeds poured over the top just before serving. It is cheap, filling, and freezes well.
sourceNotes: Dahl has been eaten across the Indian subcontinent for thousands of years. The tarka -- spiced hot oil added at the end -- is a technique found across Indian cooking and is what distinguishes a good dahl from a plain lentil soup.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes very well for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Excellent for batch cooking. Doubles easily.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for 5 days. Reheat with a splash of water.

content.text: The tarka is poured over the dahl at the very end. Have everything else ready before you make it -- the oil needs to be hot and go on immediately.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Cook the onion for 8 minutes until golden. Add the garlic, ginger, and ground spices. Cook for 2 minutes.
Add the lentils, tinned tomatoes, and 800ml water. Season with salt. Bring to a simmer.
Cook for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils are very soft and the dahl has thickened. Add more water if needed.
Stir in the lemon juice. Taste and adjust seasoning.

Make the tarka: heat 3 tablespoons of oil in a small pan until very hot. Add the sliced garlic and fry for 30 seconds until golden. Add the cumin seeds and chilli flakes -- they will sizzle immediately. Pour straight over the dahl.
Serve with rice, flatbread, or naan.

items.symptom: Lentils are still firm after 30 minutes
items.cause: Not enough water or old lentils
items.fix: Add 200ml more water and continue simmering. Old dried lentils take longer to soften.
Simmer uncovered until it thickens to the consistency you want.

content.text: Dahl is eaten daily across South Asia and has been for thousands of years. The word means lentil or pulse in Sanskrit. Every region has its own version -- some smooth, some textured, some made with red lentils, some with green or black. The tarka -- the sizzling spiced oil poured over at the end -- is the defining finishing touch and gives the dish its distinctive aroma.
